sections.heading: Partial fractions with an irreducible quadratic factor

questions.q: Set up (but do not solve for constants) the partial fraction decomposition of $\frac{3x^2+2}{(x-1)(x^2+4)}$.
questions.answer: Since $x^2+4$ is irreducible over the reals, the decomposition has the form $\frac{A}{x-1}+\frac{Bx+C}{x^2+4}$.

questions.q: Evaluate $\int_0^1\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,dx$, or show it diverges (note the integrand is undefined at $x=0$).
Evaluate $\int_0^2\frac{1}{(x-2)^2}\,dx$, or show it diverges (the integrand is undefined at $x=2$).
State the p-test for $\int_1^{\infty}\frac{1}{x^p}\,dx$, and use it to determine convergence for $p=3$ and $p=0.5$.
questions.answer: $\int_1^{\infty}\frac{1}{x^p}\,dx$ converges if $p>1$ and diverges if $p\leq1$. For $p=3>1$: converges. For $p=0.5\leq1$: diverges.

questions.q: State the analogous p-test for $\int_0^1\frac{1}{x^p}\,dx$ (a discontinuity at $x=0$), and determine convergence for $p=\frac{1}{2}$ and $p=2$.
questions.answer: $\int_0^1\frac{1}{x^p}\,dx$ converges if $p<1$ and diverges if $p\geq1$ (opposite condition from the infinite-limit case). For $p=\frac{1}{2}<1$: converges. For $p=2\geq1$: diverges.

sections.heading: Combining partial fractions with improper integrals

questions.answer: $\frac{1}{(x+1)(x+2)}=\frac{1}{x+1}-\frac{1}{x+2}$. $\int_0^{b}\left(\frac{1}{x+1}-\frac{1}{x+2}\right)dx=\left[\ln\frac{x+1}{x+2}\right]_0^b=\ln\frac{b+1}{b+2}-\ln\frac{1}{2}$. As $b\to\infty$, $\frac{b+1}{b+2}\to1$, so the limit is $\ln1-\ln\frac{1}{2}=\ln2$. Converges to $\ln2$.

$\frac{6x^2-3x-1}{x(x-1)(x+1)}=\frac{A}{x}+\frac{B}{x-1}+\frac{C}{x+1}$. $6x^2-3x-1=A(x-1)(x+1)+Bx(x+1)+Cx(x-1)$. At $x=0$: $-1=-A \Rightarrow A=1$. At $x=1$: $2=2B \Rightarrow B=1$. At $x=-1$: $8=2C \Rightarrow C=4$. So $\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{x-1}+\frac{4}{x+1}$.

sections.heading: Visualizing convergence: area under the curve

questions.q: The convergent improper integral $\int_1^{\infty}\frac{1}{x^2}\,dx=1$ (shown earlier) means the infinite region under $y=\frac{1}{x^2}$ for $x\geq1$ has FINITE area. Explain intuitively why this is possible even though the region extends forever.
questions.answer: Even though the region is infinitely long, the height $\frac{1}{x^2}$ shrinks fast enough as $x\to\infty$ that the accumulated area still converges to a finite total — the 'tail' contributes less and less area, summing to a bounded amount, similar to how a convergent geometric series sums to a finite value despite infinitely many terms.

questions.q: By contrast, $\int_1^{\infty}\frac{1}{x}\,dx$ diverges. Compare the graphs of $y=\frac{1}{x}$ and $y=\frac{1}{x^2}$ on $[1,10]$ and explain why $\frac{1}{x}$ decays too slowly for the area to stay finite.
questions.answer: Both curves decrease, but $\frac{1}{x}$ stays larger than $\frac{1}{x^2}$ for all $x>1$ (e.g. at $x=10$: $0.1$ vs $0.01$). This slower decay means the accumulated area under $\frac{1}{x}$ keeps growing without bound as $x\to\infty$, while $\frac{1}{x^2}$'s faster decay allows its total area to converge.

sections.heading: Improper integrals with both an infinite bound and a discontinuity

questions.q: Evaluate $\int_0^{\infty}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}(1+x)}\,dx$ is a classic doubly-improper integral (discontinuous at $x=0$ AND infinite upper bound). Explain how such an integral must be split to evaluate it.
questions.answer: Split at any convenient interior point, e.g. $x=1$: $\int_0^{\infty}=\int_0^1+\int_1^{\infty}$. Each piece is evaluated as its own limit (one with $a\to0^+$, the other with $b\to\infty$), and the original integral converges only if BOTH pieces converge.

questions.q: Use a direct comparison to argue that $\int_1^{\infty}\frac{1}{x^2+1}\,dx$ converges, without computing it exactly.
questions.answer: For $x\geq1$: $\frac{1}{x^2+1}<\frac{1}{x^2}$. Since $\int_1^{\infty}\frac{1}{x^2}\,dx$ converges (shown earlier, $p=2>1$), and the given integrand is smaller and positive, $\int_1^{\infty}\frac{1}{x^2+1}\,dx$ also converges by comparison.

questions.q: Use a direct comparison to argue that $\int_1^{\infty}\frac{2+\sin x}{x}\,dx$ diverges.
questions.answer: Since $-1\leq\sin x\leq1$, we have $2+\sin x\geq1$, so $\frac{2+\sin x}{x}\geq\frac{1}{x}$ for $x\geq1$. Since $\int_1^{\infty}\frac{1}{x}\,dx$ diverges, and the given integrand is at least as large, $\int_1^{\infty}\frac{2+\sin x}{x}\,dx$ also diverges by comparison.

questions.q: Evaluate $\int_0^1\frac{1}{x^{\frac{2}{5}}}\,dx$, or show it diverges (the integrand is undefined at $x=0$).
questions.answer: Since $p=\frac{2}{5}<1$, this converges (by the $p$-test at a discontinuity). $\int_0^1x^{-\frac{2}{5}}\,dx=\lim_{a\to0^+}\left[\frac{x^{\frac{3}{5}}}{\frac{3}{5}}\right]_a^1=\frac{1}{\frac{3}{5}}-0=\frac{5}{3}$.

questions.q: Evaluate $\int_0^1\frac{2}{x^{\frac{1}{4}}}\,dx$, or show it diverges (the integrand is undefined at $x=0$).
questions.answer: Since $p=\frac{1}{4}<1$, this converges (by the $p$-test at a discontinuity). $\int_0^12x^{-\frac{1}{4}}\,dx=\lim_{a\to0^+}\left[\frac{2x^{\frac{3}{4}}}{\frac{3}{4}}\right]_a^1=\frac{2}{\frac{3}{4}}-0=\frac{8}{3}$.

questions.q: Evaluate $\int_0^1\frac{1}{x^{\frac{3}{4}}}\,dx$, or show it diverges (the integrand is undefined at $x=0$).
questions.answer: Since $p=\frac{3}{4}<1$, this converges (by the $p$-test at a discontinuity). $\int_0^1x^{-\frac{3}{4}}\,dx=\lim_{a\to0^+}\left[\frac{x^{\frac{1}{4}}}{\frac{1}{4}}\right]_a^1=\frac{1}{\frac{1}{4}}-0=4$.

questions.q: Evaluate $\int_0^1\frac{2}{x^{\frac{1}{2}}}\,dx$, or show it diverges (the integrand is undefined at $x=0$).
questions.answer: Since $p=\frac{1}{2}<1$, this converges (by the $p$-test at a discontinuity). $\int_0^12x^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,dx=\lim_{a\to0^+}\left[\frac{2x^{\frac{1}{2}}}{\frac{1}{2}}\right]_a^1=\frac{2}{\frac{1}{2}}-0=4$.

questions.q: Evaluate $\int_0^1\frac{6}{x^{\frac{1}{5}}}\,dx$, or show it diverges (the integrand is undefined at $x=0$).
questions.answer: Since $p=\frac{1}{5}<1$, this converges (by the $p$-test at a discontinuity). $\int_0^16x^{-\frac{1}{5}}\,dx=\lim_{a\to0^+}\left[\frac{6x^{\frac{4}{5}}}{\frac{4}{5}}\right]_a^1=\frac{6}{\frac{4}{5}}-0=\frac{15}{2}$.

choices: Diverges only because $a=4$ happens to be even.
Diverges, since $\frac{4+\sin x}{x}\geq\frac{3}{x}$ for $x\geq1$, and $\int_1^{\infty}\frac{3}{x}\,dx$ diverges since $p=1\leq1$.
Converges, since $\frac{4+\sin x}{x}\leq\frac{5}{x}$ for $x\geq1$, and $\int_1^{\infty}\frac{5}{x}\,dx$ converges since $p=1>1$.
Cannot be determined by comparison, since $\sin x$ oscillates.
